titre: William Jones, 1786: A Sentence About Sanskrit
accroche: The sentence that passes for the birth certificate of Indo-European was uttered in passing, in a speech about something else, and it was not the first.
contenu_vulgarise:
On February 2, 1786, in Calcutta, William Jones delivers the third annual discourse of the Asiatic Society of Bengal, of which he is president. The topic of the day: the Hindus, their country, their religion, their letters. In the middle of the talk, after describing the territory where the religion of Brahma holds sway, Jones slips in a sentence that would become one of the most quoted in all of linguistics. He writes “Sanscrit,” in the old spelling, and the sentence runs to about ten printed lines. The next one already speaks of the nâgarî script.

## What the Sentence Asserts

Jones judges Sanskrit to be “of a wonderful structure,” “more perfect than the Greek, richer than the Latin.” This compliment is a scholar's taste, not an argument. The argument comes next: Sanskrit resembles Greek and Latin, he says, “in the roots of verbs and in the forms of grammar,” more than chance could produce. He is not talking about isolated words that look alike; he is talking about the way verbs are built and conjugated. No philologer examining the three languages, he concludes, could avoid believing that they “sprung from some common source, which, perhaps, no longer exists.”

He adds, with a caution the text retains, that there is a similar reason, though a weaker one, for connecting Gothic and Celtic to the same origin, and that Old Persian might be added to them “if this were the place” to discuss the antiquities of Persia.

## What It Does Not Assert

Two misreadings circulate. The first has Jones say that Sanskrit is the mother language of Greek and Latin. The text says the opposite: the three languages are sisters, descended from a source that may have disappeared. The second makes Jones the inventor of the idea. He is only its most audible mouthpiece: others had noted the kinship before him, notably Marcus Zuerius van Boxhorn in 1653 and the Jesuit Gaston-Laurent Cœurdoux in 1767, according to his biography in the online encyclopedia Wikipedia.

## The Shift

What distinguishes the sentence of 1786 is, first, a criterion: kinship is proved by grammar, not by the resemblance of a few words, which may be due to chance or borrowing. It is, next, a falsifiable hypothesis: if a common source exists, one should be able to deduce forms from it. The sentence is more a work program than a result. Jones does not say what the vanished language looked like, and does not say how to recover it. The historical linguistics of the following century would be built in large part on that second point.

citation.source: The Third Anniversary Discourse, delivered February 2, 1786 to the Asiatic Society of Bengal, published in Asiatick Researches, vol. 1, 1788

carte.punch: Jones never wrote that Sanskrit is the ancestor of Latin.
carte.idee: In 1786, William Jones observes that Sanskrit, Greek, and Latin resemble each other in their verb roots and grammar, too much for it to be chance. He infers a common source, perhaps vanished: sisters, not mother and daughters.

quiz.question: What does Jones conclude, in 1786, from the fact that Sanskrit, Greek, and Latin resemble each other in their verb roots and grammar?
choix: That Sanskrit is the language from which Greek and Latin descend through gradual simplification
That the three languages come from a common source that perhaps no longer exists
That Greek and Latin borrowed their verbs from Sanskrit through commercial contacts
That only the vocabulary is related, the grammar of each language being its own
quiz.explication: Jones writes that the three languages may have sprung from a common source, perhaps vanished. He does not make Sanskrit an ancestor, and he does not speak of borrowings: he judges that the resemblance of verb roots and grammar exceeds what chance would produce.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why does Jones stress the roots of verbs and the forms of grammar rather than vocabulary?
choix: Because isolated words can resemble each other by chance or borrowing, but a whole grammar cannot
Because Sanskrit vocabulary was then too poorly known to be compared
Because grammar is the oldest and noblest part of languages
Because Greek and Latin verbs all come from Sanskrit
quiz_supplementaire.explication: A resemblance in a few words is explained by chance or borrowing. A resemblance in the way verbs are made is harder to attribute to anything other than a shared origin, hence the strength of the argument.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Was Jones the first to note this kinship?
choix: Yes, no similar remark existed before his 1786 discourse
No: Boxhorn in 1653 and Cœurdoux in 1767, among others, had already noted it
Yes, but only for Greek and Latin, never for Sanskrit
No, but his predecessors published nothing
quiz_supplementaire.explication: His name remains attached to the sentence because the discourse was widely read, not because the idea was new. Others had formulated and published it before him.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which phrase of the sentence prevents reading “Sanskrit is the mother language” into it?
choix: “sprung from some common source, which, perhaps, no longer exists”
quiz_supplementaire.explication: A common source that perhaps no longer exists places Sanskrit on the same level as Greek and Latin, as sisters. The compliment about its perfection is an aesthetic judgment, not a lineage.
